newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak star quits in state interference protest.
newsitem.headline: Slovak star quits in state interference protest.

text.p: International opera star Peter Dvorsky has quit the Slovak National Theatre to protest against what he calls government interference in the arts, a leading Bratislava daily newspaper said on Thursday.
Dvorsky, a Slovak tenor, linked his decision to resign after 24 years with the recent sacking of National Theatre director Dusan Jamrich by Culture Minister Ivan Hudec.
"I have left because I don't agree with this cultural policy ...I am afraid I cannot accept this any more," the independent daily Pravda quoted Dvorsky as telling the Bratislava-based Radio Twist.
Dvorsky has a villa in Bratislava but travels extensively abroad to sing and has recently performed at the Vienna State Opera. Telephone calls to his home here were not being answered on Thursday.
The acting profession is the latest group with which the government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar has locked horns.
Earlier this month, National Theatre actors went briefly on strike to protest against Jamrich's removal and other government moves which they say constitute government interference in the arts.

Meciar is also at odds with President Michal Kovac, the opposition, the independent media, leaders of Slovakia's Hungarian minority, the medical profession and from time to time his coalition partners.
Dvorsky said he would not return to the National Theatre unless action was taken over Jamrich, who was replaced by Miroslav Fischer, manager of the Chamber Opera.
"They (government officials) would have to apologise to him and then advertise a normal competition for both the posts of director and general manager of the opera," Dvorsky said.

An estimated 10,000 people demonstrated in Bratislava recently over the government's arts policyand at least 35,000 have signed a petition protesting against state interference in the autonomy of cultural institutions and demanding that Hudec resign.
Actors suspended their stoppage after three days but remained on a strike alert.

Meciar's reaction was blunt. "We have more state-sponsored theatres than other nations...All of them choose any drama they wish, any art direction and cast they want, they show what they want," he told a recent rally.
Playing on nationalist dislike of the neighbouring Czech Republic, he said: "If they want to kiss arses in Prague, let them do it, but don't let them consider this Slovak culture."
This appeared to be a veiled reference to a piece by Czech playwright Karel Steigerwald in which one of the actors kisses his partner's back on stage.

Artists and intellectuals have always enjoyed high respect among Slovaks and Czechs, joined until Czechoslovakia split at the end of 1992, and wield greater moral authority than in many other countries.
They have been outspoken in their criticism of the Meciar government which they say is increasingly authoritarian.
